content_voiceover: Clinically, G6PD deficiency presents as acute hemolytic anemia and, in newborns, neonatal jaundice. When you're asked what precipitates hemolysis, the answer boards want is infection, that's actually the most common trigger, more common than drugs. Other precipitants are certain drugs, diabetic acidosis, and fava beans, particularly relevant in Mediterranean and Asian variants where favism is classic. For diagnosis, you screen with the fluorescent spot test and confirm with quantitative spectrophotometric analysis measuring actual enzyme activity. Two testing pitfalls are frequently tested. First, testing during or immediately after acute hemolysis can be falsely negative, because the older, more enzyme-deficient red cells have already been destroyed, leaving a population of young cells and reticulocytes that have relatively higher G6PD activity, so you need to retest weeks later. Second, female heterozygotes can be difficult to diagnose because of X-chromosome mosaicism, or lyonization, meaning they have a mixed population of normal and deficient red cells that can average out to a falsely normal result. Treatment is supportive: remove the offending oxidant, give folic acid, and transfuse if the anemia is severe.
keypoints: Infection = most common hemolysis trigger (more than drugs)
Screen: fluorescent spot test; confirm: quantitative spectrophotometry
Testing during acute hemolysis can be falsely negative — retest later
Female heterozygotes: falsely normal due to X-inactivation mosaicism (lyonization)
Treatment: remove trigger, folic acid, transfusion if severe
